questions.stem: The nurse is observing care for a client on contact precautions for vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE). Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Leaving a disposable blood pressure cuff in the room for this one client's use
Using the unit's shared stethoscope, then wiping it with an alcohol pad
Putting on a gown and gloves before entering the room to change the bed linens
Removing the gown and gloves inside the room before stepping out into the hallway

rationale.correct: Contact precautions: gown and gloves on entry, dedicated equipment, removing PPE before leaving and thorough cleaning of anything shared.

perOption.a: Dedicated equipment is correct for contact precautions.
perOption.b: Shared equipment should be avoided; VRE survives on surfaces, and the stethoscope should stay in the room or be fully disinfected per policy.
perOption.c: Gown and gloves are required for contact with the client or the environment.
perOption.d: PPE is removed before leaving the room.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Maintain contact precautions for a resistant organism.

questions.stem: A client who received chemotherapy 9 days ago calls the oncology clinic. The client feels tired and has a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) but says, "I feel okay otherwise. Can I just take acetaminophen and wait?" What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: Take acetaminophen, drink extra fluids and call back if the fever lasts more than 24 hours
Come to the emergency department now for blood tests, cultures and IV antibiotics
Recheck the temperature in 4 hours and come in if it reaches 39 °C (102.2 °F)
Schedule a clinic appointment for tomorrow morning to have a white blood cell count drawn

rationale.correct: Fever of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher after chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic fever: same-day evaluation, cultures and IV antibiotics within an hour.

perOption.a: Fever in a client with likely neutropenia is an emergency; waiting can be fatal.
perOption.b: Day 7 to 14 after chemotherapy is the usual low point for white cells; neutropenic fever needs antibiotics within an hour.
perOption.c: 38 °C or higher is enough to act on in a client who may be neutropenic.
perOption.d: Waiting until tomorrow delays life-saving antibiotics.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to fever after chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A nurse arrives for a shift with an active cold sore (herpes labialis) on the lip. Which assignment should the charge nurse avoid giving this nurse?

options.text: A client with pneumonia who is being discharged home later today
A client with extensive partial-thickness burns on the burn unit
A client with a fractured ankle who is waiting for surgery
A client with COPD who is receiving nebulizer treatments

rationale.correct: Staff with active herpes labialis should not care for high-risk clients such as newborns, people with burns and people who are severely immunocompromised.

perOption.a: With careful hand hygiene and covering the lesion, routine care of most adults is acceptable.
perOption.b: Herpes simplex can cause severe infection in burn wounds, newborns and people who are immunocompromised.
perOption.c: This client is not at special risk.
perOption.d: This client is not at special risk for herpes infection.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Make assignments for a nurse with a cold sore.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary tuberculosis has been on airborne precautions and four-drug therapy for 3 weeks. Which finding supports ending airborne precautions?

options.text: The client has completed 14 days of therapy and has a lower temperature
Three negative AFB sputum smears and improving symptoms on therapy
The client's tuberculin skin test is now negative after 3 weeks of treatment
The client wears a surgical mask whenever staff are in the room

rationale.correct: Airborne precautions for TB can end with three negative AFB sputum smears, clinical improvement and effective therapy.

perOption.a: Time on therapy alone is not enough; smear results are needed.
perOption.b: Negative smears with clinical improvement on treatment show the client is unlikely to be infectious.
perOption.c: Skin tests stay positive after infection and do not show infectiousness.
perOption.d: Masking does not end the need for airborne isolation.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Decide when to end airborne precautions.

questions.stem: After a busy morning caring for a client receiving IV chemotherapy who also has a draining wound and needs insulin, the nurse has several used items. For each item, indicate where the nurse should dispose of it.

rows.text: Gloves and gown worn while giving IV chemotherapy
A dressing soaked with blood from a wound
The paper wrapper from a sterile dressing kit

rationale.correct: Sort waste by hazard: sharps containers for needles, hazardous drug waste for chemotherapy items, biohazard bags for blood-soaked items and regular trash for clean packaging.

perOption.r1:c1: Needles go in a sharps container.
perOption.r1:c2: Insulin is not a hazardous drug.
perOption.r1:c4: Needles are never put in regular trash.
perOption.r2:c2: Items contaminated with hazardous drugs go in hazardous drug waste.
perOption.r2:c3: Biohazard bags are for infectious waste, not chemotherapy.
perOption.r2:c4: Chemotherapy-contaminated items are not regular trash.
perOption.r3:c3: Blood-soaked items go in a biohazard bag.
perOption.r3:c4: Saturated items are not regular trash.
perOption.r4:c4: Clean packaging goes in regular trash.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Dispose of clinical waste correctly.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old client taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation slipped in the bathroom and hit their head 30 minutes ago. The client is alert, oriented and says, "I'm fine, just a bump." There is a small bruise on the forehead. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply ice to the bruise and check on the client again at the end of the shift
Notify the provider and expect a head CT and frequent neurological checks
Hold the next apixaban dose and let the client rest without disturbing them overnight
Document the fall as minor, since the client is alert and denies pain

rationale.correct: Older adults taking anticoagulants who strike their head need provider notification, usually CT imaging and frequent neurological checks.

perOption.a: Anticoagulated clients can bleed into the brain slowly; checks at the end of the shift are too late.
perOption.b: Older adults on anticoagulants who hit their head need imaging and close monitoring, even with no symptoms at first.
perOption.c: Changing doses needs a prescription, and the client needs monitoring, not undisturbed rest.
perOption.d: Normal findings early do not rule out a delayed bleed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a head strike in an anticoagulated client.

questions.stem: During a safety round on a pediatric unit, the nurse checks four rooms. Highlight the findings that need correcting.

cells: Crib side rail lowered while the parent steps out to the bathroom
A latex balloon from a visitor tied to the bed
Call light clipped to the pillow and within reach
Small building blocks the size of a marble on the bedside table
Bed in the lowest position with the wheels locked

rationale.correct: Pediatric safety: crib rails up when unattended, no latex balloons, no small objects for toddlers, call light within reach and beds low and locked.

perOption.r1: Crib rails must be up whenever the child is in the crib and no one is at the bedside.
perOption.r2: Latex balloons are a choking hazard and can cause allergic reactions.
perOption.r4: Small toys are a choking hazard for toddlers.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify safety hazards on a pediatric unit.

questions.stem: A client with a seizure disorder is sitting in a chair when a generalized tonic-clonic seizure begins. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the client's arms and legs firmly to keep them from injuring themselves
Ease the client to the floor, protect the head and turn them onto their side
Place a padded tongue blade between the client's teeth to protect the tongue
Leave the client briefly to get the prescribed IV lorazepam from the medication room

rationale.correct: During a seizure: protect from injury, lower to the floor, turn to the side, time the seizure and stay with the client; never restrain or put anything in the mouth.

perOption.a: Restraining movements can cause fractures and other injuries.
perOption.b: Lowering the client prevents a fall, and side-lying keeps the airway clear of secretions.
perOption.c: Nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.
perOption.d: The nurse stays with the client and calls for help.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client at 28 weeks of gestation who is Rh-negative and had a normal 1-hour glucose screen at 24 weeks comes for a prenatal visit. The client received a Tdap vaccine during a pregnancy 2 years ago. Which intervention should the nurse expect today?

options.text: Repeat the 1-hour glucose challenge test
Give Tdap vaccine and Rho(D) immune globulin as prescribed
Skip the Tdap, since the client was vaccinated during the last pregnancy
Give the MMR vaccine to protect against rubella before the birth

rationale.correct: At 27 to 36 weeks, give Tdap in every pregnancy; at 28 weeks, give Rho(D) immune globulin to unsensitized Rh-negative clients.

perOption.a: A normal screen at 24 weeks does not need repeating at 28 weeks without a new reason.
perOption.b: Tdap is given in every pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks), and an unsensitized Rh-negative client receives Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks.
perOption.c: Tdap is given in each pregnancy so antibodies pass to the newborn.
perOption.d: MMR is a live vaccine and is not given during pregnancy.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care at a 28-week prenatal visit.

questions.stem: A healthy newborn is going home 18 hours after birth. The parent asks whether the newborn metabolic screen (heel stick) can be done now before they leave. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: The test can be done now, and the result will be accurate at any age
Do it before discharge and repeat it within about 2 weeks
The test can be skipped because the baby looks healthy and is feeding well at the breast
The test has to wait until the baby is 1 month old at the first clinic visit

rationale.correct: Newborn screening is ideally done after 24 hours of age; early discharge needs a repeat screen within about 2 weeks.

perOption.a: Testing before 24 hours can miss some conditions, such as phenylketonuria.
perOption.b: Screens done before 24 hours of age need a repeat test so conditions are not missed.
perOption.c: Most screened conditions cause no symptoms at first.
perOption.d: Waiting that long delays diagnosis of treatable conditions.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain newborn screening timing.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old will be in the hospital for 3 weeks for treatment of osteomyelitis. Which activity best supports the child's developmental stage?

options.text: Watching cartoons on the television in the room for most of the day
Keeping up with schoolwork and doing a project the child can finish
Being held and rocked by a parent to provide comfort and closeness
Playing alone with a stuffed animal and pretend medical toys

rationale.correct: School-age children build competence through schoolwork, projects, hobbies and contact with peers.

perOption.a: Passive activity does not support the sense of accomplishment children seek at this age.
perOption.b: School-age children are in Erikson's industry versus inferiority stage; completing tasks builds competence.
perOption.c: Comfort is important, but this does not target the developmental task of this age.
perOption.d: Solitary pretend play fits younger children better.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support development in a hospitalized school-age child.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with a BMI of 31 has a fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL and an A1C of 6.1%. The client asks how to keep from getting diabetes. Which goal is most strongly supported by evidence?

options.text: Cut out bread, rice and pasta for 3 months and then recheck the A1C level
Lose about 7% of body weight and do 150 minutes of activity a week
Start insulin now at a low dose so the pancreas can rest and recover
Check fingerstick glucose four times a day to watch for any changes

rationale.correct: Prediabetes: about 7% weight loss and 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; metformin may be considered for some.

perOption.a: Very restrictive diets are hard to maintain and are not the evidence-based goal.
perOption.b: The Diabetes Prevention Program showed this lowers progression from prediabetes to diabetes by more than half.
perOption.c: Insulin is not used to prevent type 2 diabetes in prediabetes.
perOption.d: Frequent glucose checks are not the key preventive step in prediabetes.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach diabetes prevention.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing breast cancer risk with a 42-year-old client. Which factors increase the client's risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: A mother diagnosed with breast cancer at 44
First menstrual period at age 10
Breastfeeding two children for a year each
Drinking two to three glasses of wine most nights
Exercising for 45 minutes most days of the week
A known BRCA2 gene mutation

rationale.correct: Breast cancer risk rises with family history, BRCA mutations, early menarche, alcohol and obesity after menopause; exercise and breastfeeding lower it.

perOption.a: A first-degree relative with breast cancer, especially young, raises risk.
perOption.b: Early menarche increases lifetime estrogen exposure.
perOption.c: Breastfeeding lowers risk.
perOption.d: Alcohol increases breast cancer risk.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify breast cancer risk factors.

questions.stem: A client who takes a combined oral contraceptive is started on rifampin for latent tuberculosis. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Take the pill 2 hours after the rifampin each day so they do not interact
Use a backup method such as condoms during rifampin and for 28 days after
Double the contraceptive pill dose during the rifampin treatment
Stop the pill until the rifampin course is finished, then restart it

rationale.correct: Rifampin reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives; advise a reliable backup or another method during and for 28 days after treatment.

perOption.a: Separating the times does not prevent this interaction.
perOption.b: Rifampin speeds up metabolism of contraceptive hormones and makes the pill less effective.
perOption.c: Doubling hormones is not recommended and may not restore effectiveness.
perOption.d: Stopping leaves the client without protection unless another method is used.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about a contraceptive drug interaction.

questions.stem: A postpartum client who is not immune to rubella also received Rho(D) immune globulin after birth. The client is going home tomorrow. What should the nurse plan?

options.text: Wait to give the MMR vaccine until the 6-week postpartum visit because of the immune globulin
Give the MMR vaccine before discharge and teach the client to avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks
Skip the MMR vaccine because the client is breastfeeding the newborn
Give the MMR vaccine and tell the client to stay away from the newborn for a week

rationale.correct: Give MMR postpartum to non-immune clients before discharge (immune globulin may lower the response, so a titer can be checked later) and advise avoiding pregnancy for 4 weeks.

perOption.a: MMR is still given before discharge; a later titer can check the response.
perOption.b: Postpartum MMR is recommended before discharge; pregnancy is avoided for 4 weeks after the live vaccine.
perOption.c: MMR is safe during breastfeeding.
perOption.d: The vaccine virus is not spread to the infant; separation is not needed.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.educationalObjective: Plan postpartum rubella vaccination.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening clients before routine vaccines. For each situation, indicate whether the vaccine should be given today.

rows.text: Inactivated influenza vaccine for an adult with hives after eating eggs
Varicella vaccine for a child receiving chemotherapy for leukemia
DTaP for a 4-month-old with a runny nose and a temperature of 37.8 °C (100 °F)
A second dose of a vaccine for a client who had anaphylaxis after the first dose

rationale.correct: Contraindications include anaphylaxis to a previous dose and live vaccines in severe immunosuppression or pregnancy; egg allergy and mild illness are not contraindications.

perOption.r1:c1: Egg allergy of any severity is no longer a reason to withhold flu vaccine.
perOption.r1:c2: Egg allergy is not a contraindication.
perOption.r2:c1: Live vaccines can cause severe infection with this degree of immunosuppression.
perOption.r2:c2: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression.
perOption.r3:c1: A mild illness is not a reason to delay vaccines.
perOption.r3:c2: Mild illness is not a contraindication.
perOption.r4:c1: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose is a contraindication.
perOption.r4:c2: The dose should not be given.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Screen for vaccine contraindications.

questions.stem: A client plans to spend a summer day at the beach. Which sun-protection advice is correct?

options.text: Use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, reapplied often and after swimming
Apply sunscreen once in the morning, since one coat lasts the whole day at the beach
Skip sunscreen on cloudy days, when the sun's rays cannot reach the skin
Use a tanning bed first to build a base tan that protects the skin

rationale.correct: Sun safety: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher reapplied every 2 hours and after swimming, shade during midday hours and protective clothing; avoid tanning beds.

perOption.a: Broad-spectrum sunscreen must be reapplied often, especially after swimming or sweating.
perOption.b: Sunscreen wears off and needs reapplying.
perOption.c: UV rays pass through clouds.
perOption.d: Tanning beds increase skin cancer risk.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach sun protection.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client admitted 2 days ago for pneumonia was calm and oriented on admission. Tonight the client is pulling at the oxygen tubing, shouting that people are hiding in the closet and cannot focus on the nurse's questions. SpO2 is 84% because the nasal cannula has slipped off, and the client has not slept since admission. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Expected confusion from being in a new place

actions.text: Replace the oxygen and correct the hypoxemia
Reorient calmly, involve family and protect sleep at night
Apply wrist restraints so the client cannot pull at the tubing
Give a scheduled benzodiazepine every 6 hours for agitation
Keep the lights on and the television running all night

parameters.text: Attention and orientation using a tool such as the CAM
Body weight measured once a week
Bowel sounds in four quadrants each shift

rationale.correct: Delirium is acute and usually has reversible causes such as hypoxemia, infection, drugs and sleep loss; treat the cause, use non-drug measures and monitor attention.

perOption.c1: A sudden change in attention and awareness with hallucinations and agitation in an acutely ill older adult is delirium; hypoxemia and sleep loss are likely causes.
perOption.c2: Dementia develops over months to years; the client was oriented 2 days ago.
perOption.c3: Schizophrenia does not begin suddenly at 76 during an acute illness.
perOption.c4: Hallucinations and inattention are not expected and need a search for causes.
perOption.a1: Hypoxemia is a reversible cause of delirium and the immediate threat.
perOption.a2: Non-drug measures are first-line for delirium.
perOption.a3: Restraints worsen delirium and are a last resort.
perOption.a4: Benzodiazepines often worsen delirium in older adults.
perOption.a5: Constant stimulation disrupts sleep and worsens delirium.
perOption.p2: Hypoxemia is a key cause to correct and track.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and manage delirium.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with major depression started sertraline 10 days ago. The parent says the teen now has more energy, is cleaning out their room and gave a favorite guitar to a friend. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the parent this is a good sign that the sertraline is starting to work
Ask the teen directly about thoughts of suicide and whether there is a plan
Suggest the parent let the teen have more time alone to rest and recover
Advise the parent to stop the sertraline because it is causing these changes

rationale.correct: Young people starting antidepressants need close monitoring for suicidality; increased energy and giving away possessions are warning signs.

perOption.a: Rising energy before mood improves, with giving away possessions, can mean higher suicide risk.
perOption.b: Antidepressants carry a warning for suicidality in young people early in treatment; these behaviors need direct assessment.
perOption.c: Isolation increases risk.
perOption.d: Stopping suddenly is not advised; the teen needs assessment.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize suicide risk early in antidepressant treatment.

questions.stem: A client admitted after witnessing a violent crime cannot move the legs. Neurological exams and imaging are normal, and the client seems calm about the paralysis. A functional neurological (conversion) disorder is diagnosed. Which approach should the nurse take?

options.text: Tell the client the paralysis is not real and they can walk if they try
Meet physical needs and focus talk on stressors, not the symptom
Order more tests until a physical cause for the paralysis is found
Leave the client to manage their own care so that they are pushed to start walking

rationale.correct: In functional neurological disorder, meet physical needs, avoid focusing on the symptom and help the client identify and cope with stressors.

perOption.a: The symptoms are real to the client and are not under voluntary control.
perOption.b: Supporting the client and exploring the stressor, without emphasizing the symptom, helps recovery.
perOption.c: Repeated testing reinforces the symptom once disease has been ruled out.
perOption.d: Withholding help is punitive and unsafe.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Care for a client with functional neurological disorder.

questions.stem: A client who takes methadone 90 mg daily for opioid use disorder is admitted for an open fracture and needs surgery. The client asks, "Will I still get my methadone?" What should the nurse expect?

options.text: The methadone will be stopped, since the client will receive other opioids for pain
The daily methadone dose will be continued, with added pain medication as needed
The client will receive half the methadone dose to lower the risk of oversedation
The client will get no opioids of any kind, to avoid triggering a relapse

rationale.correct: Continue maintenance methadone or buprenorphine during hospitalization and treat acute pain with additional analgesics.

perOption.a: Stopping methadone causes withdrawal and does not treat pain well.
perOption.b: Maintenance methadone prevents withdrawal; acute pain needs additional analgesia, often at higher doses.
perOption.c: Cutting the dose can cause withdrawal.
perOption.d: Withholding pain treatment is unsafe and does not prevent relapse.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A firefighter who pulled children from a burning building 2 months ago comes to the clinic. Which findings suggest post-traumatic stress disorder? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nightmares about the fire several nights a week
Avoiding the street where the fire happened
Startling easily at loud noises
Looking forward to returning to full duty next month
Feeling numb and detached from family
A normal appetite and steady weight

rationale.correct: PTSD symptoms last more than a month and include re-experiencing, avoidance, negative mood and thinking, and hyperarousal.

perOption.a: Re-experiencing is a core PTSD symptom.
perOption.b: Avoidance is a core symptom.
perOption.c: Hyperarousal is a core symptom.
perOption.d: This suggests coping, not PTSD.
perOption.e: Negative changes in mood and thinking are part of PTSD.
perOption.f: This is not a PTSD symptom.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize symptoms of PTSD.

questions.stem: During a school health visit, a 10-year-old tells the nurse that an adult relative has been touching them in private places and says, "Please don't tell anyone, or I'll get in trouble." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I promise I won't tell anyone, so you can tell me everything."
"You were right to tell me. I need to tell people who keep kids safe."
"Are you sure? Sometimes we misunderstand what grown-ups mean."
"Tell me exactly what happened, with each detail, so I can write it down."

rationale.correct: When a child discloses abuse: stay calm, believe and thank the child, do not promise secrecy, avoid leading questions and report as required by law.

perOption.a: The nurse cannot keep this secret and must not promise to.
perOption.b: Believing the child, praising the disclosure and being honest about reporting supports the child; the nurse must report.
perOption.c: Doubting the child can stop further disclosure.
perOption.d: Detailed questioning is left to trained forensic interviewers.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client has given birth to a stillborn baby at 36 weeks. The parents are crying quietly in the room. Which nursing action is most supportive?

options.text: Take the baby away quickly so the parents are not upset by seeing the baby
Offer time to see and hold the baby and to keep mementos
Tell the parents they are young and can try for another baby soon
Move the parents to a room next to the nursery so they can be near other babies

rationale.correct: After perinatal loss, offer choices to see, hold and name the baby and to keep mementos; place the family away from healthy newborns.

perOption.a: Many parents want time with their baby; removing the baby can complicate grief.
perOption.b: Seeing and holding the baby and keeping mementos helps many parents grieve.
perOption.c: This dismisses the loss of this baby.
perOption.d: Being near healthy newborns can increase distress.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support parents after a stillbirth.

questions.stem: A client who is an Orthodox Jew is admitted on a Friday afternoon and says they will not operate electrical devices during the Sabbath, from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall. Which plan respects the client's practice and safety?

options.text: Explain that hospital rules require the client to use the call light and bed controls as usual
Plan more frequent rounds and adjust the bed and lights for the client during the Sabbath
Disconnect the call light so the client is not tempted to use it
Ask the client to delay any needed care until the Sabbath has ended

rationale.correct: Respect religious practices by adapting care, such as more frequent rounding and staff help with devices, without compromising safety.

perOption.a: This ignores the client's religious practice.
perOption.b: Staff can provide help so the client does not need to use devices, while keeping the client safe.
perOption.c: Removing the call light is unsafe.
perOption.d: Needed care continues; most traditions allow care to protect health.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Adapt care for religious practice.
